notes.b: A landscape is shaped by two opposing sets of forces acting over very long periods. Endogenetic forces come from inside the Earth and push the land up (uplift). Exogenetic forces act at the surface and wear it down (denudation, the lowering of land by weathering, erosion and transport).
points: When uplift stops, denudation slowly lowers the land towards base level (the lowest level to which rivers can cut down, usually sea level), so the land is gradually worn down.
Cyclic landscape development means the landscape passes through a sequence of stages, from uplift to near-flatness.
A new uplift, or a fall in base level, gives the rivers fresh cutting power and so starts the sequence again.
notes.tip: Exams ask about the balance between endogenetic and exogenetic forces through time. Say that uplift and denudation oppose each other and that the balance can change.

notes.b: One model of cyclic development is the geographical cycle, also called the cycle of erosion. It was set out by William Morris Davis, an American geographer, who published it in 1899.
points: Davis's model assumes rapid uplift followed by a long period of stability, during which rivers and weathering wear the land down. The uplift is treated as a single quick event so that the wearing down can be followed stage by stage.
Davis held that the landscape depends on structure (the type and arrangement of the rocks), process (what is wearing the land down) and stage (time, how far through the cycle it is).
Davis's stages describe a whole landscape changing through time: youth, maturity and old age. Do not confuse them with the upper, middle and lower courses of one river, though the landforms overlap.
notes.tip: Davis's stages (youth, maturity, old age) describe a whole landscape. Don't confuse them with the upper, middle and lower courses of one river.

notes.b: Youth is the first stage, just after uplift. The land is high and the rivers have plenty of energy to cut downwards.
points: The landscape is an uplifted plateau with high relief (a large height difference between hills and valley floors). Gradients are steep, so rivers cut vertically downwards (vertical erosion).
Valleys are deep and V-shaped, with waterfalls and rapids, because the rivers are still cutting down through uneven rock.
Wide, flat interfluves (the areas between rivers) are not yet eroded, and there are few tributaries (small rivers that join a bigger one) because the drainage network has had little time to develop.
notes.tip: Name the landforms of each stage; you don't need to re-explain how each one forms.

notes.b: In maturity the rivers have cut down as far as they usefully can in places and begin to work sideways. The landscape is at its most dissected.
points: Relief is at its maximum, meaning the difference in height between the highest ground and the valley floors is greatest.
Valleys widen by lateral erosion (sideways cutting into the banks), so meanders (bends in the river) and floodplains (flat land beside the river that floods) develop.
The drainage network (the pattern of the main river and its tributaries) is fully developed, and interfluves are reduced to ridges because streams have cut into them from both sides.

notes.b: In old age the land has been worn down almost to base level, and the rivers have little energy left to cut. The end product of the whole cycle is the peneplain.
points: Relief is low, with very wide floodplains, large meanders, oxbow lakes (curved lakes left when a meander is cut off) and levees (natural raised banks built up along the river by floods).
Rivers flow sluggishly close to base level, because they have almost no slope left to flow down. Divides (the high ground separating one river basin from the next) are lowered to gentle rises.
A peneplain is the end product: a gently undulating surface of low relief close to base level, almost a plain. Its name means 'almost a plain'.
notes.tip: Exams ask what a peneplain is. Say it is a near-flat landscape of low relief, worn down close to base level by long-continued erosion, and that it is the end stage of Davis's cycle. A peneplain is not a floodplain (a depositional surface beside a river) and not a plateau of lava.

notes.b: Erosion does not always lower every part of the land equally. Harder rock can survive as a high point on an otherwise flat surface.
points: Monadnocks are isolated residual hills (hills left standing after the land around them was worn away) of more resistant rock rising above the peneplain.
The term comes from Mount Monadnock, New Hampshire, USA.

notes.b: Davis's cycle does not always run to its end. If the land is raised again or sea level falls, the rivers have a steeper slope to cut down, and the cycle restarts.
points: Uplift, isostatic rebound (the land rising as the weight of ice or eroded material is removed) or a fall in sea level rejuvenates the rivers (gives them renewed cutting power).
This starts a new cycle before the old one is finished. There is more on this in Fluvial adjustment to base level (Rivers).
A landscape with remnants of more than one cycle is polycyclic, because surfaces from earlier cycles survive beside the newer ones.

notes.b: Long-continued erosion can leave behind a distinctive flat surface. If that surface is later raised, it can still be recognised in the landscape.
points: A planation surface is a flat erosion surface cut across rocks of different types and structures, so its flatness is not controlled by the rock beneath.
An uplifted peneplain survives as a plateau, or as summits at similar heights (accordant summits) that cut across folded rock.
An uplifted peneplain is no longer near base level, because the land has been raised since it formed.
notes.tip: A peneplain is an erosion surface of low relief near base level. Say 'former' or 'uplifted' when describing the Munster surfaces.

notes.b: Davis's model is useful, but geomorphologists (scientists who study landforms) have questioned several of its assumptions. Know both the criticisms and the strength.
points: Walther Penck, a German geomorphologist, argued that uplift and denudation happen at the same time, not one after the other as Davis assumed.
The time needed for the cycle is far too long to observe, so the model cannot be tested directly.
The model ignores climate change, glaciation and the isostatic response to erosion (the land rising as material is removed).
Few, if any, true peneplains exist today at sea level.
In its favour, the model gives a simple, useful framework for describing landscapes by stage.

notes.h: Planation surfaces in Munster: structure and planation
notes.b: Munster is the Irish case study for planation surfaces. First the rocks were folded, then a long period of denudation cut across the folds to leave a near-level surface.
points: Folding about 300 million years ago (Variscan, also called Armorican) formed east-west ridges of Old Red Sandstone (anticlines, the upfolds) and valleys of softer Carboniferous limestone (synclines, the downfolds).
Over a very long period of denudation, the region was worn down towards a near-level surface cutting across the folds.
Evidence: flat or gently sloping upland surfaces, and summit levels at similar heights, cut across folded rocks of different types.
Diagram cue: a cross-section of folded rock with a flat planation surface cutting across the ridges and valleys.
notes.tip: A possible 30-mark question asks you to explain cyclic landscape development, or to describe how a landscape shows the balance between uplift and denudation, with reference to Munster.

notes.h: Planation surfaces in Munster: uplift and drainage
notes.b: The Munster surface was not left at base level. It was uplifted, and the rivers began cutting down again, which re-exposed the ridges and valleys. The odd course of the rivers has a usual explanation, but it is not a proven fact.
points: Later uplift raised the planation surface, and the rivers were rejuvenated (given new cutting power) and cut down again.

Renewed erosion removed the softer limestone faster than the sandstone, so the ridge-and-valley relief was re-exposed. This is differential erosion (rocks of different hardness wearing away at different rates).
The Munster Blackwater flows east through Mallow, Fermoy and Lismore, then turns sharply south at Cappoquin, Co. Waterford, to reach the sea at Youghal.

The usual explanation for the southward turn is superimposed drainage: the river first flowed south across an older surface above the present rocks, and kept its course as it cut down into the folded rocks below. This is the usual explanation, not a proven fact.
The Munster landscape is temporarily out of balance: uplift has outpaced denudation, so an old surface survives at height while the rivers are still adjusting.
notes.tip: Present superimposed drainage as 'the usual explanation', not a proven fact. To show a landscape out of balance, say that uplift has outpaced denudation and the rivers are still adjusting.

keyTerms.definition: The sequence of landscape stages from uplift to near-flatness, restarted by a new uplift or fall in base level.
W. M. Davis's model of a landscape passing through youth, maturity and old age after a period of rapid uplift.
The area of land between two rivers.
A gently undulating erosion surface of low relief, worn down close to base level by long-continued erosion.
An isolated residual hill of more resistant rock rising above a peneplain.
A landscape with remnants of more than one erosion cycle.
A flat erosion surface cut across rocks of different types and structures.
Summits at similar heights that cut across folded rock, showing an uplifted erosion surface.
Erosion that removes softer rock faster than harder rock, re-exposing relief.
Rivers that keep courses cut across older rocks as they cut down into the folded rocks below.

factCards.term: Davis's cycle of erosion: who, when and its key assumption
factCards.definition: William Morris Davis, an American geographer, published the geographical cycle in 1899. It assumes rapid uplift followed by a long period of stability while rivers and weathering wear the land down; landscape depends on structure, process and stage (time).

factCards.term: Davis's youth stage: what the landscape looks like
factCards.definition: An uplifted plateau with high relief; steep gradients and vertical erosion; deep V-shaped valleys with waterfalls and rapids; wide, flat interfluves not yet eroded; few tributaries.

factCards.term: Davis's maturity stage: what the landscape looks like
factCards.definition: Maximum relief; valleys widen by lateral erosion; meanders and floodplains develop; the drainage network is fully developed; interfluves are reduced to ridges.

factCards.term: Davis's old age stage: what the landscape looks like
factCards.definition: Low relief; very wide floodplains, large meanders, oxbow lakes and levees; rivers flow sluggishly close to base level; divides are lowered to gentle rises. The end product is a peneplain, with monadnocks of resistant rock rising above it.

factCards.term: Cycle of erosion: what interrupts it and what results
factCards.definition: Uplift, isostatic rebound or a fall in sea level rejuvenates the rivers and starts a new cycle before the old one is finished. A landscape with remnants of more than one cycle is polycyclic.

factCards.term: Davis's model: four criticisms and one strength
factCards.definition: Walther Penck: uplift and denudation act together, not in turn; the cycle is too slow to observe; it ignores climate change, glaciation and the isostatic response to erosion; few true peneplains exist at sea level. Strength: a simple framework by stage.

factCards.term: Munster: how folding created its rock structure
factCards.definition: Folding about 300 million years ago (Variscan, also called Armorican) formed east–west ridges of resistant Old Red Sandstone (anticlines) and valleys of softer Carboniferous limestone (synclines).

factCards.term: Munster planation surface: how it formed and the evidence for it
factCards.definition: Over a very long period of denudation the region was worn down towards a near-level surface cutting across the folds. Evidence: flat or gently sloping upland surfaces and summit levels at similar heights that cut across folded rocks of different types.

factCards.term: Munster: how later uplift re-exposed the ridges and valleys
factCards.definition: Uplift raised the planation surface and rejuvenated the rivers, which cut down again; renewed erosion removed the softer limestone faster than the sandstone, so the ridge-and-valley relief was re-exposed by differential erosion.

factCards.term: Munster Blackwater: its course and the usual explanation for its turn
factCards.definition: It flows east through Mallow, Fermoy and Lismore, then turns sharply south at Cappoquin, Co. Waterford, to the sea at Youghal. The usual explanation is superimposed drainage: it first flowed south across an older surface and kept that course as it cut down.

factCards.term: Munster: why its landscape is temporarily out of balance
factCards.definition: Uplift has outpaced denudation, so an old, uplifted erosion surface survives at height while the rivers are still adjusting by cutting down.

questions.prompt: Describe and explain the stages in cyclic landscape development.
questions.model: Davis's model assumes rapid uplift followed by a long period of stability, during which rivers and weathering wear the land down. In youth, the uplifted plateau has high relief, steep gradients and vertical erosion, deep V-shaped valleys with waterfalls and rapids, and wide, flat interfluves that are not yet eroded. In maturity, relief is at its maximum, valleys widen by lateral erosion, meanders and floodplains develop, the drainage network is fully developed, and the interfluves are reduced to ridges. In old age, relief is low, with very wide floodplains, large meanders, oxbow lakes and levees, and rivers flow sluggishly close to base level. The end product is a peneplain, a gently undulating surface of low relief close to base level. Monadnocks, isolated residual hills of more resistant rock, rise above the peneplain. If uplift, isostatic rebound or a fall in sea level occurs before the cycle is finished, the rivers are rejuvenated and a new cycle begins, and a landscape with remnants of more than one cycle is polycyclic. One criticism is that uplift and denudation happen at the same time, as Walther Penck argued, rather than one after the other. The model also ignores climate change and glaciation, and few true peneplains exist at sea level today.

questions.prompt: Examine how the landscape of Munster shows the effects of planation and later uplift.
questions.model: Folding about 300 million years ago, the Variscan or Armorican folding, formed east–west ridges of Old Red Sandstone and valleys of softer Carboniferous limestone. Over a very long period of denudation, the region was planed down towards a near-level surface that cut across the folds. Evidence for this planation is the flat or gently sloping upland surfaces and summit levels at similar heights, cut across folded rocks of different types. Later uplift raised this planation surface, so that it is now a former peneplain away from base level. The rivers were rejuvenated and cut down again. Renewed erosion removed the softer limestone faster than the sandstone, so the ridge-and-valley relief was re-exposed; this is differential erosion. The Munster Blackwater flows east through Mallow, Fermoy and Lismore, then turns sharply south at Cappoquin, Co. Waterford, to reach the sea at Youghal. The usual explanation is superimposed drainage: the river first flowed south across an older surface above the present rocks and kept its course as it cut down through the folds. The landscape is temporarily out of balance, because uplift has outpaced denudation, so an old surface survives at height while the rivers are still adjusting.

questions.prompt: Explain briefly what is meant by a peneplain.
questions.model: A peneplain is a gently undulating erosion surface of low relief, worn down close to base level by long-continued erosion. It is the end stage of Davis's cycle of erosion.
